identifications.body:
Several reasons. I'll start with a trait you won't find in keys:
  • In the first photo are dead spots on the leaves—spots that look simply white or tan and withered. These spots happen frequently on S. drummondii, but never on P. chinensis. That is not to say that you will never see dead spots on the leaves of P. chinensis, but only that they will not look at all like these.
  • The bark of this tree is a very light ash gray, almost white. The bark of a young P. chinensis would be cinnamon brown.
  • The branch angles on this tree are generally well less than 90°. The branch angles on P. chinensis would generally be very close to 90°—in fact, the angles will occasionally be obtuse!
  • The smaller branches are quite crooked. On P. chinensis, they would be quite straight.
So rather than one of the worst invasive trees in recent history, this is a valuable native.

results.description:
Went down to Giddings for the funeral of my grandfather -- he lived to be 100 years old!  Imagine the changes in the world in the last 100 years...  He had a full life, and that's something to be quite grateful for.

I observed a few birds on the way down, and then we stopped at the 'farm house' where my grandfather and my father was born.  It was nice to connect with lots of family here too.

Fruits were translucent although hard to see in photo.

Tree growing out of truck!
I love this photo!  I'm so sorry for the loss of your grandfather, but I'm grateful that you had many good years with him and many good memories.
Thanks Suzette!  Yeah, it was a really full life that he had -- I have great memories of spending time at this farm too.  :)  The plants and nature have pretty much taken over though!

Great photo of rural central Texas. Not far from Old Evergreen.  
Agree it is soapberry.  One of the plants my TMN friend Katherine @doodlebug in Milam Co. loved.
